# Effects of Pistachio Consumption on Cognition, Cardiometabolic Risk Factors, and Life Satisfaction in Older Adults: Protocol for a Remote-Based Randomized Controlled Trial

**Authors:** Sarah Jaehwa Park; Irene Sanchez Gavilan; Sidong Li; Allison Clar; Jessica Lau; Grace C. Karbowski; Ara A. Sarkissian; Montaña Cámara; Howard D. Sesso

**Affiliations:** aDivision of Preventive Medicine, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA. | bOsher Center for Integrative Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA. | cReal colegio Complutense at Harvard University, Boston, MA, USA. | dDepartment of Nutrition and Food Science, Complutense University of Madrid, Spain. | eDepartment of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA.

## Abstract

Pistachios contain key nutrients and bioactive compounds that may be particularly relevant for cognition health. Although short-term pistachio intervention trials have demonstrated improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors implicated in cognitive decline, the potential cognitive effects of pistachio consumption remain to be adequately elucidated.

This remote-based, 6-month randomized controlled trial will test the effects of a pistachio-enriched diet (1.25 oz/d), compared to usual diet, on cognitive function in older US adults (target n=80). Key eligibility criteria include: active participation in the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS), age 65–80 years, current nut intake of ≤1 serving/week, and being free of dementia or recent cardiovascular disease, cancer, or changes in relevant medications. The primary outcome is Mobile Toolbox fluid cognition composite scores, derived by averaging standardized test scores across five domains (associative memory, episodic memory, working memory, processing speed, executive function). Secondary outcomes include individual cognitive domain scores, cardiometabolic risk factors (body weight, waist circumference, blood pressure, fasting glucose, lipids, interleukin-6, insulin-like growth factor 1), and life satisfaction.

Results from this trial will contribute to the growing literature on the cardiometabolic effects of pistachio consumption and may offer insight into its potential role in cognitive function, life satisfaction, and the mechanisms by which it could influence these interrelated domains of health in older adults. Findings will be interpreted in the context of a modest sample size and other pragmatic study design considerations.

This trial is registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Identifier: NCT06992544).

## INTRODUCTION

Nutrition is an important modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disorders through its influence on underlying biological pathways, including oxidative stress, inflammation, vascular dysfunction, and cardiometabolic abnormalities.1,2 The Mediterranean and Mediterranean-Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay (MIND) diets are the most extensively studied dietary patterns in relation to cognitive outcomes and have been associated with lower risks of cognitive impairment, dementia, and Alzheimer’s disease (AD).3–5 To that end, research has increasingly focused on whether specific foods within these patterns, such as nuts, may independently contribute to observed benefits. This manuscript describes the rationale and design for a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to test the effects of a pistachio-enriched diet on cognitive function, cardiometabolic risk factors, and life satisfaction in older US adults.

### Background and rationale

Tree nuts are abundant in protein, dietary fiber, healthy fats, and an array of vitamins, minerals, and phytochemicals with potential neuroprotective properties.6 Several studies have shown that nut intake is associated with better cognitive function,7–12 although RCTs testing the cognitive effects of specific nuts have yielded mixed results.13–23 Given the variability in nutrient composition among nut types, it is plausible that certain nuts may confer greater neurocognitive benefits than others. Pistachios, in particular, have garnered increasing attention for their unique combination of nutrients and bioactive compounds, many of which may be particularly relevant for cognitive health.

Among all nuts, pistachios contain the highest levels of γ-tocopherol, vitamin K, potassium, phytosterols, and carotenoids such as lutein, zeaxanthin, and β-carotene.24,25 They are also an excellent source of protein, fiber, unsaturated fatty acids, B vitamins, phosphorus, magnesium, copper, and polyphenols, while having one of the lowest caloric densities among nuts. Despite their favorable nutritional profile, pistachios have been largely overlooked in cognitive research. Walnuts have been evaluated in a meta-analysis of five RCTs, which found no significant effect on global cognitive function, although some included studies suggested that higher intake levels (30–60 g/day) may be beneficial for certain cognitive subdomains and population subgroups.23 Almonds have been tested in fewer trials with similarly inconsistent results.18–21 In contrast, no RCTs have yet examined the potential neurocognitive benefits of pistachios. Preclinical studies suggest that pistachio supplementation may protect against drug- and diet-induced cognitive and motor impairments.26,27 Yet, the limited human evidence for pistachios consists of one nonrandomized pilot trial reporting that consuming 28 g/day for four weeks improved individual cognitive domains,28 and one cross-sectional analysis of NHANES data showing no significant association with cognitive function.29

Although the cognitive effects of pistachios remain unclear, there is a strong mechanistic basis to support their potential protective role. Pistachios contain high levels of tocopherols, carotenoids, and polyphenols, which may influence cognitive function through antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and vascular pathways.30–33 Pistachio consumption has been shown to improve markers of oxidative stress, inflammation, endothelial function, and vascular stiffness.28,34–39 In a crossover RCT of adults with hypercholesterolemia, consuming 1–2 daily servings of pistachios for four weeks increased serum concentrations of γ-tocopherol, lutein, β-carotene while lowering oxidized low-density lipoprotein (oxLDL).38 Importantly, higher circulating levels of these antioxidants have been linked to more favorable cognitive outcomes,40–42 with lutein also appearing to modulate the influence of vascular stiffness on cognitive function.43

Pistachios may also support cognitive health in part through improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors. The beneficial effects of pistachio consumption on blood pressure (BP), lipid profiles, and glycemic control are well-established,44–50 which likely reflects a combination of nutrients and bioactive compounds common to many nuts. Pistachios may offer a distinct advantage for reducing BP and lipids due to their exceptionally high potassium and phytosterol content. In a meta-analysis comparing the effect of various nut types on BP, pistachios were the only single nut intervention associated with significant reductions in either systolic or diastolic BP (SBP and DBP, respectively).49 Similarly, pistachios demonstrated the greatest reductions in total cholesterol (TC), low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), and triglycerides (TG), with walnuts and almonds showing the second-largest improvements in these parameters.50

Beyond traditional clinical and biological outcomes, maintaining psychological well-being and quality of life is increasingly recognized as a key component of healthy aging. Life satisfaction, a global measure of one’s feelings and attitudes about their life as a whole, has been associated with lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults.51–53 It may also influence cognitive function indirectly by promoting healthier dietary choices and fostering psychological processes that support cognitive resilience.53,54 Pistachio consumption has been associated with improvements in dietary intake,55–57 better mood state,28 and lower likelihood of anxiety and depression,29 although its effects on life satisfaction remains poorly understood. Because nutrition affects not only physical health but also mood, energy, and overall well-being, evaluating life satisfaction alongside cognitive and cardiometabolic outcomes may provide a more comprehensive understanding of the potential benefits of pistachio consumption.

### Objectives

The primary aim of this trial is to evaluate whether a pistachio-enriched diet, compared to usual diet, leads to changes in cognitive function in older adults over a 6-month period. Additionally, given the links between cognitive function, cardiometabolic health, and psychological well-being, our secondary aim is to evaluate whether the pistachio-enriched diet concurrently leads to changes in cardiometabolic risk factors and life satisfaction.

## METHODS

### Overall trial design

This is a pragmatic remote-based, parallel-arm, open-label RCT to test the effects of a pistachio-enriched diet, compared to usual diet, on 6-month changes in cognitive function, cardiometabolic risk factors, and life satisfaction in older US adults (target n = 80). The parallel-arm design and trial duration ensure we can reliably and adequately evaluate any changes in cognitive function beyond the practice effects by trial participants when taking neurocognitive tests, typically undermining cross-over designs with wash-out periods. Assessments will be conducted at baseline, 3 months (subjective adherence and adverse events only), and 6 months via the MyCap application (for cognitive assessments), REDCap questionnaires (for life satisfaction, adherence, adverse events, dietary, and other phenotypic assessments), and at local Quest Diagnostics sites (for biometric measurements and biospecimen collection, which will be returned to our biorepository). After all baseline assessments are completed, participants will be randomized to either the pistachio-enriched diet or usual diet group. The participant flow chart is shown in Figure 1.

The trial was approved by the Mass General Brigham (MGB) Institutional Review Board (IRB #2024P002479, approved 20 January 2025), and informed consent will be obtained for all participants prior to enrollment. Funding for this study was provided by the American Pistachio Growers, who had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, or interpretation.

### Recruitment

We will recruit participants from the COcoa Supplement and Multivitamin Outcomes Study (COSMOS; ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02422745), a completed randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled, two-by-two factorial trial with ongoing observational follow-up. The trial design and baseline characteristics of COSMOS participants have been previously described.58–60 Briefly, COSMOS recruitment included mailings to active Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) Extension Study participants61; women and men contacted for, but not randomized into, the VITamin D and OmegA-3 TriaL (VITAL)62; and mass mailings and media outreach across the US. A total of 21,442 older adults were randomized into COSMOS between June 2015 and March 2018, including 12,666 women aged ≥65 years and 8,776 men aged ≥60 years initially free of myocardial infarction, stroke, and recently diagnosed cancer (except for nonmelanoma skin cancer) within the past two years.

In the present study, we will recruit from a pool of 6,867 potentially eligible COSMOS participants who completed the year 2 semiquantitative food frequency questionnaire (SFFQ) and reported “rarely/never” or “<1 serving/week” for peanut, walnut, and other nut consumption to select participants with low baseline intake levels. Unlike COSMOS, which used sex-specific minimum ages based on the original recruitment patterns of WHI/VITAL, we will apply the same age range for all participants, as recruitment for the present trial is limited to a single cohort.

### Eligibility criteria

Eligibility criteria for trial participation are summarized in Figure 2. Inclusion criteria include: being an active COSMOS participant, aged 65 to 80 years, and residing in US states other than Arizona, Hawaii, or Wyoming (as there are no Quest Diagnostics sites in these three states). Exclusion criteria include: having a tree nut allergy; current pistachio, peanut, walnut, and other nut intake (not including nut butters) >1 serving/week; diagnosis of AD or dementia; diagnosis of cancer or cardiovascular disease (defined as myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary artery bypass grafting, percutaneous transluminal coronary angiography, or stent) within the 12 months prior to prescreen; changes in the dose or number of anti-hypertensive, lipid-lowering, or diabetic medications over the three months prior to prescreen; and not owning a smartphone or tablet device.

Participants will also be excluded if they report being unable or unwilling to: abstain from pistachio consumption or limit nut intake to ≤1 serving/week for six months, complete online questionnaires and cognitive assessments, travel to a local Quest site for biospecimen collection, or provide consent to participate in the trial. Additionally, enrolled participants will be excluded prior to randomization if they fail to complete the baseline life satisfaction questionnaire, cognitive assessments, and biospecimen collection.

### Randomization

A total of 80 participants will be randomized to the pistachio-enriched diet or usual diet (control) group on a rolling basis in a one-to-one ratio (n=40/group), using a block randomization scheme with fixed blocks of four. The allocation sequence will be generated by a study programmer who is not involved in participant recruitment or outcome assessment.

### Interventions

The pistachio group will be asked to consume 1.25 oz/day (≈35 g; ~200 kcal) of shelled, roasted, and unsalted pistachio kernels during the 6-month intervention period. This dose was selected as a pragmatic addition to participants’ usual diet rather than a dietary substitution to balance feasibility and caloric burden. Although prior trials show that pistachio consumption (≈1.5 oz/day for up to four months) can be compensated for through spontaneous dietary adjustment without weight gain, these studies were generally shorter in duration.56,57 A modestly lower daily dose was therefore chosen to reduce the risk of cumulative excess energy intake over six months while preserving potential benefits. Participants will receive pre-portioned 1.25-oz pistachio packets in two 3-month shipments and be instructed to consume the full packet each day as a snack, incorporated into meals, or divided across the day according to preference. A website link with pistachio-based recipes will also be provided.

The control group will be asked to continue their usual diet while abstaining from pistachio consumption and limiting other nut intake to ≤1 serving/week to maintain a clear distinction between intervention and control conditions during the 6-month intervention period. While abstinence from all nuts would increase the differences between the intervention groups, we will limit non-pistachio nut intake in the control group to ≤1 serving/week (with no nut consumption strongly preferred) to improve willingness to participate, trial retention, and risk minimization. Participants will not be asked to limit consumption of nut butters during the intervention period. As a recruitment incentive, the control group will be sent a one-time shipment of pistachios after trial completion.

### Primary outcome: Cognitive function

The primary outcome is cognitive function, as measured by the Mobile Toolbox (MTB) fluid cognition composite (FCC) score.63 The MTB, based on the well-validated NIH Toolbox cognitive battery (NIHTB-CB),64,65 is a remote smartphone-based, self-administered battery that includes six tests measuring “fluid” cognitive domains (associative memory, episodic memory, working memory, processing speed, and executive function) and two tests measuring “crystalized” cognition (language). This study focuses exclusively on fluid cognition because it relies on biological processes and declines with advancing age, while crystalized cognition primarily reflects accumulated knowledge over the lifespan and tends to remain stable throughout adulthood.66,67

Participants will be asked to download the MyCap application on their personal smartphone or tablet device to complete the six MTB fluid cognition tests: Face and Names, Arranging Pictures, Sequences, Arrow Matching, Shape-Color Sorting, and Number Symbol Match.68–72 We will construct the FCC score, as previously described by Jutten et al,68 by standardizing scores for each MTB test using means and standard deviations (SD) across the entire sample and averaging z-scores across the six tests (mean=0; SD=1). Higher FCC scores will indicate better cognitive function.

### Secondary outcomes

#### Individual cognitive domains

We will secondarily assess scores in the five aforementioned cognitive domains individually. Associative memory will be measured by the Face and Names test, which includes three tasks (Face Seen Before, Face Name Letter, and Face Name Matching) that are summed for a total possible score range of 0 to 36.69 Episodic memory will be measured by the Arranging Pictures test, which is scored as the sum of adjacent pairs correctly placed across two trials (range: 0–26).72 Working memory will be measured by the Sequences test, which yields a raw score for the total number of items correctly answered (range: 0–30).70 Similarly, the Number-Symbol Match test, a measure of processing speed, provides a raw score for the total number of items correctly answered in 90 seconds (range: 0–144).71 Executive function will be measured as the summative total of two tests: Arrow Matching for inhibitory control and Shape-Color Sorting for cognitive flexibility. Each test is scored as the number of correct trials divided by the total testing time and then summed for a total possible score range of 0 to 20.71

#### Cardiometabolic risk factors

Additional secondary outcomes include cardiometabolic risk factors and life satisfaction. Cardiometabolic assessments include: body weight (in kg), waist circumference (in cm), seated SBP and DBP (in mmHg), lipid profile (in mg/dL for TC, LDL-C, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol [HDL-C], TG), fasting plasma glucose (FPG; in mg/dL), serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1; in ng/mL), and serum interleukin-6 (IL-6; in pg/mL). Participants will be sent a blood collection kit to take to their local Quest Diagnostics site for biometric measurements and biospecimen collection using standard procedures. Serum IGF-1 and IL-6 will be measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) from R&D Systems (Minneapolis, MN).

#### Life satisfaction

Life satisfaction will be assessed via REDCap using the Life Satisfaction Index for the Third Age-Short Form (LSITA-SF),73,74 a validated self-rated 12-item assessment of successful aging and psychological well-being among older adults. Participants will be instructed to select an answer that most closely reflect their attitude towards each statement on a Likert scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree). A summative total will be calculated (range: 6–72), with higher scores indicating greater life satisfaction. All primary and secondary outcomes will be assessed at baseline and 6-month follow-up.

#### Other prespecified outcomes

Because participants in the pistachio group are instructed to add pistachios to their habitual diet rather than substitute specific foods, no prespecified dietary replacements will be mandated. However, to evaluate whether pistachio consumption is associated with any dietary changes (e.g., total energy intake, displacement of other foods), participants will complete the Harvard SFFQ75 via REDCap at baseline and 6-month follow-up, where they will indicate the average amount of each specific item that they have consumed over the preceding six months (never or less than once per month, 1–3 per month, 1 per week, 2–4 per week, 5–6 per week, 1 per day, 2–3 per day, 4–5 per day, >6 per day).

We will also evaluate treatment adherence via serum lutein (in μmol/L) and γ-tocopherol (in mg/L) levels (as part of the Quest Diagnostics biospecimen collection) at baseline and 6 months, using an Alliance high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system (e2695 Separation Module) equipped with Waters 2998 photodiode array detector. Previously, a 4-week crossover RCT showed that consuming 1–2 daily servings of pistachios increased serum lutein and γ-tocopherol concentrations,38 thus, we expect them to be reliable biomarkers of pistachio intake. The pistachio group is expected to have increases in serum lutein and γ-tocopherol levels, while the control group is expected to have no changes. Lastly, we will administer 3- and 6-month REDCap questionnaires to subjectively evaluate treatment adherence and related challenges (e.g., taste, amount, etc.) and adverse events. The timeline of all outcome assessments is summarized in Figure 3.

#### Power calculation

We used G*Power (version 3.1)76 to compute power estimates for a range of expected between-group effect sizes (Cohen’s d) for 6-month changes in MTB-FCC scores in a fixed sample size of 80 participants (Figure 4). Due to the lack of published intervention studies evaluating MTB-FCC outcomes, our power calculations were informed by lifestyle intervention trials assessing 12-week changes in NIHTB-CB FCC scores, which reported effect sizes ranging from 0.22 to 1.27.77,78 Assuming a two-arm parallel design with two-tailed α=0.05, a sample size of 80 participants provides 82% power to detect an effect size of 0.65. Given the low risk of side effects from pistachios and targeted recruitment of motivated participants from the COSMOS trial, we anticipate nonadherence and attrition will have minimal impact on our power estimates.

### Statistical analysis

For our primary aim, we will perform intention-to-treat analyses using general linear models (ANCOVA) to estimate between-group differences (95% confidence intervals) in mean 6-month MTB-FCC and individual cognitive domain scores (primary and secondary outcomes, respectively), with each outcome adjusted for its own baseline value. Standardized effect sizes will be reported as Cohen’s d (mean difference / pooled SD) using conventional benchmarks (small=0.2, medium=0.5, large=0.8).79 We will consider additional models to adjust for any unexpected imbalances in key baseline variables despite randomization. Paired t-tests will evaluate within-group changes in cognitive scores. For our secondary aim, we will estimate between-group differences in cardiometabolic risk factors (body weight, waist circumference, BP, lipids, FPG, IGF-1, IL-6) and LSITA-SF scores, closely paralleling analyses for our cognitive outcomes.

Subgroup analyses will explore whether the effect of the pistachio intervention on the primary outcome is modified by the following baseline covariates: age (above or below the median), sex (female, male), race (white, non-white), education level (high school/GED or less, attended college or above), MTB-FCC and LSITA-SF scores (above or below the median), and levels of serum lutein and γ-tocopherol, body mass index, SBP, DBP, TC, LDL-C, HDL-C, TG, FPG, IGF-1, and IL-6 (above or below the median for all). If no overall treatment effect on the primary outcome is observed, subgroup analyses may be restricted to a limited set of prespecified, biologically plausible effect modifiers. General linear models will include interaction terms between treatment and each covariate, adjusting for baseline MTB-FCC scores.

If a main treatment effect on the primary outcome is observed, we will explore potential mediators between pistachio consumption and cognitive function. Hierarchical linear models will include 6-month changes in select cardiometabolic risk factors known to respond to pistachio interventions (SBP, TC, LDL-C, TG),49,50 biomarkers of pistachio consumption (lutein and γ-tocopherol),38 and LSITA-SF score as intermediate variables. Parameter estimates from nested models will be compared to assess the degree to which changes in these intermediate factors account for potential treatment-related cognitive changes.

In the event of substantial missing outcome data at the 6-month follow-up assessment, sensitivity analyses will assume data are missing at random (MAR) and estimate missing values using multiple imputation by chained equations.80 Additional sensitivity analyses will evaluate departures from the MAR assumption, such as imputing control-group mean changes with added random error, to assess the impact of possible non-random missingness.

P values of ≤0.05 will indicate statistical significance. Given the exploratory nature of our subgroup, mediation, and sensitivity analyses, no formal correction for multiple comparisons will be applied. Thus, all results except for those of our primary analyses will be interpreted cautiously and considered hypothesis-generating. All analyses will be blinded to treatment status and performed using SAS and/or R statistical software.

### Pistachio composition testing

In collaboration with the Complutense University of Madrid, we will additionally analyze the nutritional and chemical composition of pistachios used in our trial. Samples will be collected from different boxes, with two 1.25-oz bags from each box sent for analysis. The contents of randomly selected units will be pooled and analyzed in duplicate. Nutrients and bioactive compounds such as magnesium, iron, zinc, selenium, lutein, γ-tocopherol, and fatty acids will be measured using standardized laboratory methods. Statistical analyses, including ANOVA and t-tests, will assess between-sample variation.

### Data management

The Brigham and Women’s Hospital (BWH) Division of Preventive Medicine will manage the long-term storage of the blood samples. De-identified samples will be stored for future biomarker studies related to cognition and cardiometabolic health. BWH will be responsible for tracking, storing, and distributing the blood samples to appropriate laboratories. For assays, BWH will coordinate with the labs for shipping, testing protocols, and receipt of results data. Data will be stored on encrypted and password-protected computers kept in secure locations at all times. A unique anonymous identifier will be assigned to each participant, and all data collected will be associated exclusively with this identifier.

### Data monitoring and safety plans

All data will undergo additional within-form and across-time checks to verify accuracy. Safety monitoring will be closely tracked during the trial through participant reports, either from planned questionnaires or spontaneous reports received by telephone or other means. We will follow standard adverse event reporting guidelines as specified by the MGB IRB. Any unexpected adverse event will be thoroughly documented and reported to the IRB per the reporting protocol. Participants will be removed from the study should they experience severe side effects or adverse events determined to be related to the intervention. Participants may also request removal from the study.

## DISCUSSION

To our knowledge, this will be the first RCT to evaluate the effects of a pistachio-enriched diet on cognitive function, cardiometabolic risk factors, and life satisfaction in older adults. This study leverages recruitment from a large trial cohort with detailed baseline data and prior engagement in remote-based research and extends prior nut intervention research by jointly assessing changes across cognitive, cardiometabolic, and psychological domains. Findings may help clarify how pistachio consumption impacts these interrelated domains of health and inform the design of larger, longer-term trials aimed at supporting healthy aging.

The trial has several limitations that warrant consideration. First, our modest sample size limits statistical power to detect small intervention effects, though it is sufficient to evaluate moderate effects. Second, the chosen pistachio dose represents a moderate, pragmatic intake aimed at enhancing adherence and minimizing excess caloric intake in an older adult population. While higher nut doses have been examined in prior studies, this approach prioritizes feasibility over maximal exposure. Moreover, this trial does not include a run-in period as participants cannot be blinded to the intervention, which could influence adherence to the pistachio intervention and introduce open-label bias.

Third, despite the MTB cognitive battery demonstrating strong reliability and validity,68–72 its use in interventional research remains limited; thus, it is unclear how sensitive test scores will be in response to the pistachio intervention. The present study will provide early evidence regarding its responsiveness to dietary modification in older adults. Fourth, generalizability may be limited, with modest racial and ethnic diversity in COSMOS and volunteer bias for those willing and eligible to enroll in a clinical trial. Moreover, completing remote-based cognitive assessments requires a smartphone or tablet and some degree of comfort in navigating technology, which may further limit generalizability to the broader older adult population. Fourth, our trial protocol does not include calibration for cognitive testing conditions (e.g., internet stability, time of day, lighting, participant distractions) or alternative MTB follow-up tests, which may contribute to variability and practice effects for MTB test scores. However, the 6-month intervention period was selected to minimize short-term practice effects, and our primary analyses will focus on between-group differences to understand whether the pistachio intervention may lead to greater cognitive improvements than usual diet.

Fifth, given the exploratory nature of all non-primary analyses, no formal adjustments will be made to correct for multiple testing. Consequently, with multiple secondary outcomes and interactions tested at the nominal 0.05 level, some significant findings may occur by chance alone. However, these results will be interpreted cautiously, and any significant findings other than for our primary outcome will be considered hypothesis-generating. Finally, although the study is supported by industry funding, study design, data collection, and analyses will be conducted independently. Nonetheless, the source of funding is acknowledged as a potential source of bias.

## Trial status and data availability

This trial began enrollment in June 2025 and is ongoing. Data are not currently available.
